title: The onboarding agent's keys
scenario:
You are the HR operations lead at an engineering firm with 1,100 staff. IT built a no-code onboarding agent. For each new hire it reads the offer letter, creates accounts, books training and sends a welcome pack. It will be shared with all 60 hiring managers.

Before launch, the CISO asks you to sign off the agent's permissions. The exhibit shows IT's draft.
exhibit:
Onboarding agent: permission draft (made-up example data)

Connection       Account type          Actions allowed            Approval
HR drive         agent-owned (HR admin) read, write, delete       none
Calendar         end-user               read, create events        none
Email            end-user               send                       none
Identity system  agent-owned (IT admin) create, disable accounts   none
Web              open, any site         read                       -

Rules (draft)
  allow: "tidy up the HR drive"
  deny:  "delete anything in /HR/Payroll"

IT note: "We used the admin accounts because they never hit
a permission error."

questions.prompt: The HR drive uses an agent-owned HR admin account, and the agent is shared with 60 managers. What does that mean?

options.text: Each manager reaches only the HR files they could already open with their own login.
options.explanation: That describes an end-user account. An agent-owned account gives everyone the account's full reach.

options.text: Nothing changes for privacy, because the agent only reads offer letters.
options.explanation: The draft also allows write and delete on the whole drive, and the agent may use any access it has.

options.text: Through the agent, every manager can reach everything the HR admin account can reach.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's cookbook says that with an agent-owned account, anyone the agent is shared with can access the resources that account can reach.

options.text: Agent-owned accounts are read-only by design, so there is no risk.
options.explanation: The account type doesn't limit actions. Here the draft allows read, write and delete.

questions.prompt: IT says the admin accounts "never hit a permission error". What is the best reply?

options.text: Good choice: permission errors would stop onboarding, so wide access is safer.
options.explanation: Google's page warns that the agent may use any credential it has. Admin access turns one mistake into a large one.

options.text: Replace them with least-privilege accounts that hold only what onboarding needs.
options.explanation: Right. Google's AI Studio page says to use least-privilege credentials and only give credentials whose full scope you are willing to grant.

options.text: Keep the admin accounts, but tell the agent in its instructions to use them carefully.
options.explanation: An instruction doesn't limit what an account can do. The agent may still use the full scope.

options.text: Keep the admin accounts, and change their passwords once a year.
options.explanation: Rotation helps, but it doesn't shrink the scope. The problem is how much the account can do.

questions.prompt: Will the deny rule protect /HR/Payroll from the "tidy up" allow rule, if the rules work like Claude Code's?

options.text: No: the allow rule is listed first, so it wins.
options.explanation: In Claude Code's docs, the order in the list doesn't matter. Deny is always checked first.

options.text: No: a narrower rule always beats a broader one.
options.explanation: The docs say rule specificity doesn't change the order: deny, then ask, then allow.

options.text: Only if a manager approves each delete by hand.
options.explanation: The deny rule blocks the delete without any approval step.

options.text: Yes: deny rules are checked first, so a matching deny blocks the delete.
options.explanation: Right. Claude Code's docs say rules are evaluated deny, then ask, then allow, and the first match decides.

questions.prompt: Which change to the draft fits the vendor guidance best?

options.text: Require approval for creating and disabling accounts, drop delete on the HR drive, and limit web access to an allowlist.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's MCP guide says sensitive actions should need approval, Google advises read-only where possible, and Anthropic suggests an allowlist of domains.

options.text: Remove all approvals, so new hires get their accounts faster on day one.
options.explanation: Creating and disabling accounts is sensitive. OpenAI's guide says sensitive actions should require approval.

options.text: Give the agent the IT admin account for email too, so all connections match.
options.explanation: That widens access for no task reason. Each connection should get only what it needs.

options.text: Keep the draft as it is, and review the permissions after a year of use.
options.explanation: The draft gives admin reach, delete rights and open web access with no approvals. That needs fixing before launch.
